words.definition: The chance discovery of something pleasant while looking for an unrelated thing.
words.example: Finding my future business partner in a delayed airport line was pure serendipity.
words.mnemonic: From the fairy tale 'The Three Princes of Serendip,' who kept stumbling on lucky finds — 'Serendip' + lucky trip.

words.definition: Happening by lucky accident to produce a welcome, unplanned result.
words.example: Our meeting was entirely serendipitous — we both grabbed the last seat at the same café.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'serene + dip in' — you calmly dip into a situation and luck falls in your lap.

words.definition: Arriving as if by divine timing to help exactly when needed.
words.example: The rain was providential, dousing the wildfire moments before it reached the village.
words.mnemonic: Think 'provided by Providence' — heaven provides help right on time.

words.definition: Showing favorable conditions that make success or a good outcome likely.
words.example: With clear skies and a full moon, the sailors judged it a propitious night to set out.
words.mnemonic: 'Pro' (for you) + sounds like 'precious' — conditions are FOR you and precious to your plans.

words.definition: Happening by chance, often in a lucky or beneficial way.
words.example: It was fortuitous that the doctor happened to be dining nearby when the man collapsed.
words.mnemonic: Hiding inside is 'fortu-' like a fort of luck — chance builds a fortress around you.

words.definition: Well chosen and pleasingly appropriate for the occasion or purpose.
words.example: Her felicitous toast captured exactly what everyone felt but couldn't quite say.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'Felix,' meaning happy — a felicitous phrase makes everyone happy.

words.definition: A state of great happiness, or an aptly graceful turn of expression.
words.example: The couple spent their first months in a bubble of quiet felicity.
words.mnemonic: The name 'Felicity' comes from Latin 'felix' — happy; picture a beaming friend named Felicity.

words.definition: A helpful thing that brings welcome benefit or advantage.
words.example: The new bridge was a boon to farmers who had struggled to reach the market.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'moon' — a wish granted under the moon is a gift, a boon.

words.definition: The predetermined course of events believed to shape a person's life.
words.example: When they met again by accident years later, she smiled and called it kismet.
words.mnemonic: 'Kiss met' — the fated kiss you were always destined to meet.

words.definition: A surprising success or event produced purely by chance.
words.example: Sinking the ball off three cushions was a total fluke, and he knew it.
words.mnemonic: Picture a lucky fish (a flatfish is called a fluke) leaping into your boat by accident.

words.definition: A coincidence, or something occurring by pure random chance.
words.example: By happenstance, both strangers had booked the same cabin for the same weekend.
words.mnemonic: Literally 'happen' + 'circumstance' — a circumstance that just happens to occur.

words.definition: A sudden event causing great damage, suffering, or distress.
words.example: The flood was a calamity that left half the town without homes overnight.
words.mnemonic: 'Call a medic!' — when disaster strikes you shout for help; a calamity calls a medic.

words.definition: Causing serious harm, disaster, or deep misfortune.
words.example: The general's calamitous decision to advance in winter destroyed the entire army.
words.mnemonic: Add '-ous' to 'calamity' — full OF calamity, so a calamitous choice invites disaster.

words.definition: A violent, large-scale disaster causing sudden and sweeping destruction.
words.example: The eruption was a cataclysm that buried the coastal cities under ash within hours.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'kata-' (down) + 'klyzein' (to wash) — a great flood washing everything down.

words.definition: Relating to a sudden, violent event of enormous destructive scale.
words.example: The asteroid impact triggered cataclysmic changes that wiped out most life on Earth.
words.mnemonic: 'Cat-a-clysmic' — imagine a giant cat swatting a city flat; catastrophe on a massive scale.

words.definition: A sudden event that causes great damage, suffering, or ruin.
words.example: The oil spill was a catastrophe for every fishing village along the coast.
words.mnemonic: Greek cata- (down) + strophe (turn): a sudden turn downward, like a curtain crashing down.

words.definition: A total, humiliating failure or complete collapse of something planned.
words.example: The product launch turned into a debacle when the app crashed live on stage.
words.mnemonic: Say 'de-BUCKLE': everything comes unbuckled and falls apart at once.

words.definition: A difficult stretch of life marked by hardship, suffering, or bad luck.
words.example: She kept her sense of humor even in the face of crushing adversity.
words.mnemonic: Root ad- (toward) + vers- (turn): the world has turned against you.

words.definition: A condition of ongoing pain, illness, or deep distress.
words.example: Chronic migraines were an affliction that kept him in dark rooms for days.
words.mnemonic: From Latin fligere, 'to strike' — it flicks pain at you again and again.

words.definition: An episode that goes wrong through bad luck or a foolish mistake.
words.example: Their camping trip became a misadventure of flat tires, rain, and a lost tent.
words.mnemonic: mis- (badly/wrong) glued onto 'adventure': an outing gone wrong.

words.definition: Hard, painful labor or intense effort, often prolonged.
words.example: After months of travail, the exhausted crew finally finished building the bridge.
words.mnemonic: Looks like 'travel', but comes from Latin trepalium, a torture device — grueling toil.

words.definition: A period of great suffering, trouble, and distress.
words.example: The pioneers endured every tribulation—drought, disease, and hunger—on the trek west.
words.mnemonic: From Latin tribulum, a threshing sledge that crushes grain — troubles that grind you down.

words.definition: A well-deserved penalty that pays someone back for bad behavior.
words.example: The arrogant cheat finally got his comeuppance when the whole class caught him copying.
words.mnemonic: 'Come up' — what's been coming up to you at last, your just deserts arriving.

words.definition: A long-standing rival or force that reliably causes someone's downfall.
words.example: The detective finally cornered Moriarty, his cunning nemesis of many years.
words.mnemonic: Nemesis was the Greek goddess of retribution who punished the proud.

words.definition: A source of persistent harm, ruin, or misery.
words.example: Weeds were the bane of the gardener's summer, choking every flower bed.
words.mnemonic: Hear it in 'wolfsbane' and 'ratsbane' — old poisons that kill; a bane destroys.

words.definition: Poisonous or destructive; likely to cause serious harm.
words.example: The tabloid's baneful gossip wrecked reputations purely for entertainment.
words.mnemonic: bane (poison, as in wolfsbane) + -ful: full of poison, harmful through and through.

words.definition: A cause of widespread suffering or ruin; historically, a whip for punishment.
words.example: Cholera was the scourge of crowded cities before clean water arrived.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'scour' — it scours across a land, stripping away everything in its path.

words.definition: A difficult, distressing, or dangerous situation someone is stuck in.
words.example: News of the stranded refugees' plight prompted donations from around the world.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'tight' — being caught in a tight spot with no easy way out.

words.definition: A tricky, unpleasant situation that is hard to get out of.
words.example: Locked out in the rain with a dead phone, she pondered her predicament.
words.mnemonic: 'Predict-a-ment': a jam so bad you can't predict how you'll ever escape it.

words.definition: Unlucky and deserving of pity; forever meeting misfortune.
words.example: The hapless waiter dropped three trays before the lunch rush even began.
words.mnemonic: 'Hap' means luck (as in happen and mishap) + -less: luck-less.

words.definition: Consistently experiencing bad outcomes and misfortune through no fault of one's own.
words.example: The luckless gambler lost every hand, and then discovered his car had been towed.
words.mnemonic: Break it apart: luck + -less = 'less luck,' i.e. none to spare.

words.definition: A person or thing believed to bring bad fortune to someone.
words.example: Ever since he wore that cap to the matches, the team kept losing, so everyone called it a jinx.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'links'—picture a bad-luck link that drags down whatever it touches.

words.definition: An inevitable and terrible fate, especially ruin or death.
words.example: As the storm smashed the ship's hull, the sailors sensed their doom drawing near.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'tomb'—both echo with gloom and a grim ending.

words.definition: Complete and everlasting spiritual ruin; the state of being condemned to hell.
words.example: The preacher thundered that a life of cruelty leads straight to perdition.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'perdere' (to lose)—like Spanish 'perder,' it's losing your soul utterly.

words.definition: A sudden loss of power, wealth, or status, or its cause.
words.example: Greed proved to be the tycoon's downfall once investigators traced the missing funds.
words.mnemonic: Literally 'down' + 'fall'—picture a king tumbling down from his high throne.

words.definition: The cause of someone's ruin or defeat.
words.example: His stubborn refusal to ever ask for help was ultimately his undoing.
words.mnemonic: To 'un-do' something is to unravel it—your undoing unravels everything you built.

words.definition: A chance event, especially a lucky one occurring by accident.
words.example: By sheer fortuity, she sat down beside the very investor she had been trying to reach for months.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'fortune' inside it—fortune that arrives purely by chance.

words.definition: A situation producing great wealth, luck, or profit suddenly.
words.example: The tiny café became a bonanza the moment tourists discovered its rooftop view.
words.mnemonic: 'Bon' means good (French/Spanish)—a run of good times, like striking a rich vein of gold.

words.definition: An unexpected but very welcome and helpful thing or event.
words.example: When the neighbor offered to babysit overnight, it was a godsend for the exhausted parents.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'god-sent'—arriving as if sent from above at the exact moment you need it.

words.definition: Protective care or guidance from God, nature, or fate.
words.example: By some providence, the family had walked out of the house minutes before it collapsed.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'provide'—providence provides for you, like a watchful guardian.

words.definition: The belief that all events are fixed in advance and humans are powerless to change them.
words.example: Her fatalism meant she never planned ahead, certain that whatever came was already decided.
words.mnemonic: Fate + -ism—a whole doctrine built on surrendering to fate.

words.definition: Believing that events are predetermined and cannot be altered by effort.
words.example: He shrugged with a fatalistic calm, saying the outcome was out of his hands anyway.
words.mnemonic: The '-istic' attitude of someone who bows to fate at every turn.

words.definition: Suggesting that something bad or threatening is about to happen.
words.example: An ominous silence fell over the crowd just before the verdict was read aloud.
words.mnemonic: Spot 'omen' inside it—an omen hinting that trouble lies ahead.

words.definition: A strong feeling that something, usually unpleasant, will happen in the future.
words.example: She canceled the flight after a sudden premonition that the whole trip would end badly.
words.mnemonic: 'Pre-' (before) + 'monition' (a warning)—a warning that reaches you beforehand.

words.definition: A leading indicator that signals a coming trend or direction.
words.example: The small state is a bellwether, often voting the way the entire nation soon will.
words.mnemonic: A 'wether' is a lead sheep with a bell on its neck; the flock follows wherever it goes.

words.definition: The money or resources needed to accomplish a particular goal.
words.example: She had the talent to open a bakery but not the wherewithal to buy the ovens.
words.mnemonic: Break it into 'where-with-all': the place you get all you need to work with.

words.definition: Signaling that future events are likely to turn out badly.
words.example: Tripping on stage during the first minute was an inauspicious debut for the young actor.
words.mnemonic: 'in-' (not) + 'auspicious' (lucky, from Roman priests reading birds): the birds say no.

words.definition: Unexpected and improper or inconvenient in a way that causes difficulty.
words.example: The inspector combed the accounts for hours but found nothing untoward.
words.mnemonic: 'un-' + 'toward': things are not moving toward the proper, expected direction.

words.definition: Causing severe damage, collapse, or financial destruction to someone or something.
words.example: The failed expansion left the once-thriving bakery with ruinous debts it could never repay.
words.mnemonic: 'Ruinous' contains 'ruin' — something so bad it leaves you in ruins.

words.definition: Involving a sudden, extreme, and often irreversible disaster.
words.example: A single hairline crack in the dam could unleash catastrophic flooding on the valley below.
words.mnemonic: 'Cat-astrophe': picture a cat shoving a giant vase off a cliff — total wreckage.

words.definition: Marked by or expressing deep sadness and grief.
words.example: The cello drew out a slow, dolorous melody as the mourners filed past the coffin.
words.mnemonic: Spanish 'dolor' means pain; something dolorous is full of aching pain.

words.definition: Showing regret or sorrow, often mixed with wry self-mockery.
words.example: He gave a rueful grin as he admitted he'd locked his keys in the car for the third time.
words.mnemonic: 'Rue' means to regret; ruing your blunder leaves you rueful.

words.definition: Extremely sad, or so poor in quality as to be pitiful.
words.example: The rescue was crippled by a woeful shortage of boats and trained divers.
words.mnemonic: 'Woe' is deep sorrow; full of woe equals woeful.

words.definition: Menacing and threatening to cause harm or evil.
words.example: The old dog fixed the stranger with a baleful stare and slowly bared its teeth.
words.mnemonic: 'Bale' is an archaic word for evil or harm; a baleful glare wishes you harm.

words.definition: Extremely serious, urgent, or threatening imminent disaster.
words.example: After the earthquake, survivors were in dire need of clean water and medicine.
words.mnemonic: A blaring red 'DIRE' siren rhymes with 'fire' — drop everything and run.

words.definition: Very severe or serious, causing great pain, suffering, or harm.
words.example: He sustained grievous injuries in the crash and spent months in intensive care.
words.mnemonic: From 'grieve': a grievous wound is one bad enough to make you grieve.

words.definition: Full of danger and uncertainty; in a very risky condition.
words.example: The nation's finances were in so parlous a state that default seemed unavoidable.
words.mnemonic: 'Parlous' is a medieval squashing of 'perilous' — same peril, older spelling.

words.definition: Dangerously unstable, insecure, or dependent on chance.
words.example: The climber clung to a precarious ledge as loose rock crumbled beneath his boots.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'precari' (to pray): a precarious spot leaves you praying it holds.

words.definition: To expose someone or something to risk of harm, loss, or failure.
words.example: Skipping the pre-flight safety checks could jeopardize the entire crew.
words.mnemonic: Think of the show 'Jeopardy!' — you risk everything you've won on one answer.

words.definition: To place someone or something in danger.
words.example: Dumping the factory's waste into the river would imperil every fish for miles.
words.mnemonic: 'im-' (into) + 'peril' (danger): to put straight into peril.

words.definition: To struggle clumsily or helplessly, making little progress and losing control.
words.example: Three questions in, the nervous candidate began to flounder and lost his train of thought.
words.mnemonic: Picture a flatfish out of water, flopping and thrashing on the deck — that floundering fish is you when you're in over your head.

words.definition: To fail completely, collapse, or sink beneath the water.
words.example: The merger foundered at the last minute when the larger firm withdrew its offer.
words.mnemonic: A ship that has reached the ocean floor has 'found' the bottom — found-er, it sinks and fails.

words.definition: An urgent situation or pressing demand that requires immediate action.
words.example: Wartime exigencies forced the government to ration bread within a week.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'exit' + 'urgency' — an exigency is an urgency so sharp you need to exit and act now.

words.definition: A possible future event that cannot be predicted with certainty.
words.example: The expedition packed extra fuel and food to cover every contingency in the mountains.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'contingere,' to befall — outcomes that merely touch on us by chance, hanging on the roll of the dice.

words.definition: An unpredictable or erratic shift in behavior, mood, or circumstance.
words.example: Sailors learn to respect the vagaries of the sea, which can turn glassy to violent in an hour.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'vague' and shares the root 'vagari' (to wander) — a wandering, vague whim that strays off anywhere.

words.definition: A sudden, impulsive change of mind with no obvious reason behind it.
words.example: On a caprice, she abandoned the itinerary and boarded a train to a town she'd never heard of.
words.mnemonic: Italian 'capriccio' from 'capra,' a goat — think of a goat leaping about suddenly and unpredictably.

words.definition: A piece of bad luck or an unfortunate accident.
words.example: By sheer mischance, the only surviving negative was left in the sunlight and ruined.
words.mnemonic: Break it open: 'mis-' (bad) + 'chance' — literally a bad chance, luck gone wrong.

words.definition: An extra benefit or privilege gained from a job beyond ordinary pay.
words.example: A corner office and a driver were among the perquisites of the directorship.
words.mnemonic: This is the long form of the slangy word 'perk' — the perks of the job.

words.definition: Calm, peaceful, and happy, especially when remembering an earlier time.
words.example: The veterans reminisced about the halcyon summers before the conflict changed everything.
words.mnemonic: Named for the halcyon, a mythical kingfisher believed to calm the seas while it nested — hence serene, tranquil days.

words.definition: Deprived of something or someone, and left feeling the loss keenly.
words.example: When the last bookshop closed, the little town felt bereft of its gathering place.
words.mnemonic: It's the old past tense of 'bereave,' kin to 'reave' (to rob) — if you're bereft, you've been robbed of something.

words.definition: Good for one's health; promoting physical or mental well-being.
words.example: The doctor sent him to the coast for a month, convinced the sea breeze would be salubrious.
words.mnemonic: Shares the Latin root 'salus' (health) with 'salute' and 'salutary'; or hear 'salad-brious' — salads keep you healthy.

words.definition: Empty, bleak, and abandoned, or feeling utterly lonely and miserable.
words.example: Nothing moved across the desolate plain but the wind and a single circling hawk.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'de-sole' — left all on your own, stripped of company and warmth.

words.definition: To ruin or thwart a plan, or to sink a ship deliberately.
words.example: A single anonymous leak to the newspapers scuppered the entire peace negotiation.
words.mnemonic: A 'scupper' is the deck drain on a ship; flood water through it and you sink the vessel — you scupper it.

description: advanced and low-frequency — fortune and misfortune
